title: Kup Rahira, February 1762
hookLine: in the great holocaust, the Khalsa formed a moving ring round its families, and very many died

lines: A COLUMN AT A WALKING PACE.
cards: For years the Khalsa had stayed alive by being fast. A band of horsemen could strike and be gone before an army turned around. Speed was their shelter.

Now look at the column crossing the fields near two villages called Kup and Rahira. It isn't fast at all. It's carts and cattle and grandparents and children, moving at the pace of the slowest walker.
Riding alongside are fighters who have lived by speed, going slow on purpose. Then an army appears.

teach.h: A VAHIR: A MOVING CAMP OF FAMILIES.
teach.b: Sikhs call a moving camp of families like this a vahir: children, elders, the cooking pots, everything. The great holocaust has been told before: the surprise, the ring, the terrible losses.
Today, look at one choice inside that day.
When Abdali's army caught the vahir, the fighters had a way out. Horsemen can scatter; they'd done it for years. Split up, ride hard, regroup later.
Some of them might have got away. Tradition says they didn't.
They formed a ring around the families, fought on the outside, and kept the whole column moving forward together, at the pace of its slowest people.
Riders would turn and charge to push the attackers back, then return to the ring, again and again, all day. That's what a shield is.
Not the strongest thing on the battlefield, but the thing that stays between the danger and the ones who can't run. The cost was enormous. Very many died that day, fighters and families both.
This lesson gives no figure. It remembers the people. Why stay?
Sikh teaching holds that the Khalsa is there to protect the defenseless, and these weren't strangers. They were mothers, fathers, children.
The Ardas, said at the close of gurdwara gatherings, remembers those who gave their lives rather than give up their faith, and Sikhs hold the dead of Kup Rahira among the ones it carries.
It's not a story with a clever twist. It's a story about staying.
The fast rode slow, and they shielded the families.

how: Sikhs remember the Vadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust fought near Kup and Rahira, in the Ardas and at commemorations, honoring those who died shielding the families.

s: the fighters had no way to escape

the column kept moving forward while the fighters fought on the outside
at the pace of its slowest people, with riders charging out and returning.

games.q: you're a Sikh horseman. an army has caught your people's slow column of families in the open. your horse is fast. what do you do?
o: scatter and ride hard, as you've always done.
form a ring around the families and keep them moving.
games.why: tradition says the fighters formed a moving ring and kept the families walking all day, at a terrible cost.

practice: Sit still with your hands resting, and for the first minute keep a silence for the people of that day, fighters and families, whose names you may never learn.
Then let one person come to mind, someone you would step in front of if harm came, and just hold them there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly, at the end.

wordCard.voice: Kup Rahira. The place, named for two villages, where the Khalsa formed a moving ring around its families against Abdali's army, and very many died. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vahir, a moving camp or caravan of people with their families and belongings.

carryVoice: Your line: they shielded the families. Some days the bravest pace is the slowest one. That's day eight hundred sixty-five.
